explain.say: Imagine a football match with no rules. Anyone could grab the ball, push, or score with their hands! Look at the board. It asks why a whole country needs laws, and you and I will find four reasons together.

faq.q: What would happen with no laws?
faq.a: Pushy or strong people could take whatever they wanted, and others would not feel safe. Arguments would have no fair way to end. Laws give everyone the same protection.
asks: What if there were no rules?
Why can't we just do what we like?

faq.q: Who decides if a law was broken?
faq.a: Usually a court decides. A judge, and in some countries a jury of ordinary people, listens to both sides and then decides using the law.
asks: Who judges people who break laws?

faq.q: What is the difference between a rule and a law?
faq.a: A rule is set by a group, like your family, school or a game, and only applies there. A law is made by a government and applies to everyone in the country. Breaking a law can lead to a fine or worse.
asks: Are rules and laws the same?

faq.a: In most countries a group of elected people, called a parliament or congress, talks about new laws and votes on them. In some countries a king or one ruling party has more say.

faq.q: Do all countries have the same laws?
faq.a: No. Every country makes its own laws. Cars drive on the left in Japan, India and the UK, but on the right in the USA, Brazil and Egypt. Some ideas, like not stealing, are found almost everywhere.
asks: Are laws different in other countries?

facts: King Hammurabi's law code was carved on a stone pillar in Babylon around 1750 BCE; it is one of the oldest written law codes.
Japan, India and the UK drive on the left; the USA, Brazil and Egypt drive on the right.
